A. Its low solubility prevents acid neutralisation
B. Every basic oxide must be soluble in water
C. Copper oxide is alkaline only after melting
D. It neutralises acid but is water-insoluble [1]

(3) Which claim about limewater is chemically sound?
A. Solubility and dissociation describe different properties
B. Its pH is seven in every preparation
C. Its clear appearance establishes chemical neutrality
D. Limited solubility establishes weak dissolved-base dissociation [1]

(4) What is the usual product pattern when an acid reacts with a metal hydroxide?
A. Salt and hydrogen
B. Metal and oxygen
C. Salt and water
D. Carbon dioxide and hydrogen [1]

(5) What distinguishes a weak acid from a strong acid in water?
A. Lower concentration rather than lower ionisation
B. Partial rather than complete ionisation
C. Lower acidity at every possible concentration
D. Complete dissociation with fewer hydrogen atoms [1]

(6) Why is magnesium oxide classified as basic?
A. It necessarily contains hydroxide ions
B. It necessarily dissolves completely in water
C. It releases hydrogen with water
D. It reacts to neutralise acids [1]

(7) Why can a neutralisation mixture remain acidic?
A. The presence of water keeps the mixture acidic
B. Equal volumes necessarily mean exact neutralisation
C. Some acid may remain in excess
D. The salt formed must always be strongly acidic [1]

(8) A learner must prepare CuSO4 from warm dilute H2SO4. CuO is insoluble; NaOH is soluble. Which route is appropriate?
A. React excess CuO, filter, then crystallise
B. Add CuO, then keep the filtered solid
C. Add excess NaOH, filter and crystallise
D. React CuO, then boil the mixture completely dry [1]

(9) Which equation correctly represents magnesium oxide with hydrochloric acid?
A. MgO + 2HCl → MgCl2 + H2O
B. MgO + HCl → MgCl2 + H2
C. MgO + 2HCl → MgCl2 + CO2
D. MgO + HCl → MgCl + OH [1]

(10) Why is a precipitated insoluble salt washed after filtration?
A. To dissolve the desired insoluble product
B. To remove all the insoluble residue
C. To remove the adhering soluble impurities
D. To add further reactant to crystals [1]

(11) Which lead(II) salt is soluble in water?
A. Lead(II) carbonate
B. Lead(II) chloride
C. Lead(II) sulfate
D. Lead(II) nitrate [1]

(12) Which chloride is an insoluble exception in ordinary cold-water tests?
A. Sodium chloride
B. Silver chloride
C. Ammonium chloride
D. Potassium chloride [1]

Part 2: Correct option D (1). D. It neutralises acid but is water-insoluble. The alkali category requires water solubility. Distractor explanations: A: An insoluble base can still react with acid. B: Bases need not all dissolve in water. C: Alkalinity refers to aqueous behaviour, not merely melting. No mark for more than one selected option.

Part 3: Correct option A (1). A. Solubility and dissociation describe different properties. A low dissolved amount does not establish partial dissociation of that amount. Distractor explanations: B: Limewater is alkaline, not universally neutral. C: A clear appearance does not establish pH. D: Limited solubility does not imply weak dissociation of the dissolved hydroxide. No mark for more than one selected option.

Part 4: Correct option C (1). C. Salt and water. This is the familiar neutralisation pattern. Distractor explanations: A: Hydrogen is associated with suitable metal–acid reactions, not hydroxide neutralisation. B: Neutralisation does not produce the metal and oxygen. D: Hydroxide supplies no carbonate to generate carbon dioxide. No mark for more than one selected option.

Part 5: Correct option B (1). B. Partial rather than complete ionisation. Strength concerns extent of ionisation. Distractor explanations: A: Strength concerns degree of ionisation, not concentration. C: Concentration can vary independently of acid strength. D: A weak acid ionises partially rather than completely. No mark for more than one selected option.

Part 6: Correct option D (1). D. It reacts to neutralise acids. Acid neutralisation establishes basic behaviour. Distractor explanations: A: An oxide need not contain hydroxide ions to neutralise acid. B: Basic classification does not require complete water solubility. C: Magnesium oxide does not produce hydrogen by reacting with water. No mark for more than one selected option.

Part 7: Correct option C (1). C. Some acid may remain in excess. Neutralisation can consume only part of the initial acid. Distractor explanations: A: Water itself does not explain an excess of acid. B: Equal volumes may contain unequal reacting amounts. D: Not every salt is strongly acidic; excess acid is the stated possibility. No mark for more than one selected option.

Part 8: Correct option A (1). A. React excess CuO, filter, then crystallise. CuO supplies copper, neutralises acid, and excess solid can be removed. Distractor explanations: B: The filtered solid is excess CuO; the desired sulfate is in the filtrate. C: NaOH introduces sodium and excess dissolved alkali that filtration cannot remove. D: Boiling completely dry is not the controlled concentration-and-crystallisation route. No mark for more than one selected option.

Part 9: Correct option A (1). A. MgO + 2HCl → MgCl2 + H2O Correct formulae and atom balance give salt and water. Distractor explanations: B: Oxygen is unaccounted for and hydrogen gas is not the neutralisation product. C: No carbon source is present to form carbon dioxide. D: Magnesium chloride is MgCl2, and the neutralisation product is water. No mark for more than one selected option.

Part 10: Correct option C (1). C. To remove the adhering soluble impurities. Washing removes mother liquor and soluble contaminants. Distractor explanations: A: The aim is to retain the insoluble product, not dissolve it. B: The insoluble residue is the desired salt. D: Washing removes contamination rather than adding more reactant. No mark for more than one selected option.

Part 11: Correct option D (1). D. Lead(II) nitrate. Nitrates are soluble in the syllabus rules. Distractor explanations: A: Lead carbonate is insoluble in the stated water tests. B: Lead chloride is treated as an insoluble exception in cold water. C: Lead sulfate is insoluble. No mark for more than one selected option.

Part 12: Correct option B (1). B. Silver chloride. AgCl forms an insoluble precipitate. Distractor explanations: A: Sodium salts are soluble in the stated tests. C: Ammonium salts are soluble. D: Potassium salts are soluble. No mark for more than one selected option.

parts.canonical_answer: Use silver nitrate solution and sodium chloride solution in measured suitable amounts. Mix with stirring to precipitate AgCl; a slight excess of chloride can be used. After settling, test a separate small clear portion with an additional drop of chloride solution: no further cloudiness supports completion of silver precipitation. Filter the main mixture and keep the white AgCl residue. Wash with small portions of distilled water to remove dissolved salts, then dry between clean filter papers or by a suitable low-temperature method while protecting from strong light. The visual completion check does not prove full purity; careful washing and uncontaminated apparatus support it.
